title: Lockdowns are happening at Whitehorse jail for wrong reasons, advocates say

blocks.text: North

Inmates at Whitehorse Correctional Centre faced unscheduled lockdowns almost every second day this year, adding up to hundreds of additional hours confined to their cells. Lawyers say that affects mental health, access to programming and court proceedings.
Justice department data shows frequency of operational lockdowns at Whitehorse Correctional Centre this year
Inmates at the Whitehorse Correctional Centre faced unscheduled lockdowns more than every second day this year on average, adding up to hundreds of extra hours spent locked in their cells.
Data provided by the Yukon Department of Justice shows that inmates at the jail faced operational lockdowns on 167 of the 273 days between Jan. 1 and Sept. 30.

The lockdowns, when inmates are confined to their cells, happen because of what the department calls “operational requirements.” That can include security system or communications failures, security incidents or staffing shortages, among other things.
Inmates at the Whitehorse Correctional Centre (WCC) are scheduled to have 13 hours of “unlock” time each weekday, when they can leave their cells and access common areas.
The justice department’s data refers to unscheduled lockdowns that happen in at least one part of the facility, not necessarily the whole facility.
Yukon Legal Services Society executive director Lynn MacDiarmid says the additional lockdown time can add up to as much as 100 hours in a month.

The legal non-profit tracked time spent in unscheduled lockdowns in one unit at the correctional centre. It found that between April and August this year, inmates in that unit were spending an average of 80 hours each month in unscheduled lockdowns.
“There are lots of complaints that we receive from … the clients at WCC about the number of hours they spend locked up,” MacDiarmid said.
What does lockdown look like?
MLA Carmen Gustafson, a former lawyer and the NDP critic for justice, says she’s heard about the issue from inmates and from colleagues in the justice system.
According to Gustafson, during lockdowns people can’t access programming or use the phones to contact their lawyers or families.
“They’re really limited when those lockdowns happen,” she said. “Imagine being stuck in your house or in your bedroom and not being able to do the things that you were planning to do that day.”

NDP MLA Carmen Gustafson seen in her office earlier this year. Gustafson says that during lockdowns at the jail, inmates can’t access programming or use the phones to contact their lawyers or families. (Peter Paul Pineda/CBC)
The Department of Justice says that during operational lockdowns, Whitehorse Correctional tries to rotate unit lockups so inmates can access showers, the yard and the phones.

MacDiarmid says the extra time in lockdown affects people’s mental health. It also makes it hard for lawyers to get in touch with their clients at the facility, she says, which can delay court proceedings.
According to Yukon government data from 2024, almost 75 per cent of inmates at WCC are on remand. That means they’re awaiting trial, and have not yet been convicted of a crime.
Gustafson says inmates in the facility are often vulnerable people, many of whom have pre-existing mental health issues.
“[Whitehorse Correctional Centre] is not a big maximum security prison,” she said. “It’s a place where people should be healing and should be able to access programming.”
The Department of Justice did not provide anyone for an interview prior to publication.
Staffing 'the main issue,' says Legal Services Society
The department also didn’t provide a breakdown of how many times unscheduled lockdowns happened because of staffing shortages at the jail versus other operational limitations.
But MacDiarmid believes staffing is the main problem. She says the new correctional facility opened in 2012 and takes more resources to run.
“I think that’s the main issue…that it’s a big building, trying to keep it fully staffed.”
A 2015 report by the auditor general of Canada found that the facility needs 23 staff to run it over a 24-hour period of time.
Outside the Whitehorse Correctional Centre. (Isabel Ruitenbeek/CBC)

Vincent Larochelle, a litigation lawyer in Whitehorse, says lockdowns are legitimate if violence breaks out at the facility or some kind of intervention is needed. But he argues that correctional institutions, including the Whitehorse jail, are using them for other reasons.
Larochelle is among the lawyers with the B.C. Civil Liberties Association who’ve filed a lawsuit against the federal government to challenge its use of lockdowns in Canadian federal prisons.
“It seems to me that it's not very clear anymore why these lockdowns are being used — and they're being used routinely,” he said.
Lockdowns are an issue across Canada, to the extent that judges can take them into account during sentencing hearings.

Extra time can be taken off of a sentence if there’s evidence of harsh conditions during pre-trial custody. Harsh conditions can include lockdowns, if it’s shown that those lockdowns affected the applicant.
MacDiarmid says that’s starting to be brought up here in the Yukon.
In written sentencing decisions and appeals from the last two years in Yukon courts, CBC News found at least five cases where lockdowns were raised during sentencing.

In one, a sentencing judge dismissed lockdowns as a reason to shorten the sentence, writing that there was no context given as to how frequently lockdowns were happening at WCC, the reasons for them, the conditions during lockdown and the impact on the defendant.
Lockdown versus segregation

An investigation by the Ontario Human Rights Commission into the use of lockdowns at a facility in that province found that segregation – which means isolating inmates from others, and which is subject to strict limits and oversight – is being replaced by practices like lockdowns, that lead to similar conditions but without the associated legal protections.
That’s a problem, the report states, “because there is no evidence to suggest that the serious harms associated with solitary confinement are mitigated based on how the placement is labelled.”
Yukon’s Corrections Act includes a host of restrictions on how segregation is used.

According to the act, it’s not considered segregation if an inmate is held in isolation because the facility is temporarily locked down for security reasons, or a medical quarantine. The legislation says nothing about when those conditions are imposed due to staffing shortages or other operational requirements.
